title: Physics - Year 1 Fundamentals
description: Introductory physics covering mechanics, thermodynamics, waves, and basic electromagnetism for Year 1 university students.

questions.question_text: What is Newton's First Law of Motion?
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by an external force.

answers.answer_text: An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
Energy cannot be created or destroyed

questions.question_text: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: The Newton (N) is the SI unit of force. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

questions.question_text: What is the formula for kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv², where m is mass and v is velocity.

questions.question_text: What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: The speed of light in a vacuum is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s (299,792,458 m/s exactly).

questions.question_text: What is the relationship between wavelength (λ), frequency (f), and wave speed (v)?
questions.explanation: Wave speed equals wavelength times frequency: v = λf.

questions.question_text: What is Ohm's Law?
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law: V = IR, where V is voltage, I is current, and R is resistance.

questions.question_text: What is the acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: The acceleration due to gravity on Earth is approximately 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10 m/s²).

questions.question_text: What is the First Law of Thermodynamics?
questions.explanation: The First Law is conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted.

answers.answer_text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another
Heat flows from hot to cold objects

questions.question_text: What type of wave is sound?
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal (compression) wave - particles oscillate parallel to the direction of wave travel.

questions.question_text: What is the formula for gravitational potential energy?
questions.explanation: Gravitational PE = mgh, where m is mass, g is gravitational acceleration, and h is height.

questions.question_text: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: The Ampere (A) is the SI unit of electric current.

questions.question_text: What is the formula for work done?
questions.explanation: Work = Force × Distance × cos(θ), or simply W = Fd when force is parallel to displacement.

questions.question_text: What happens to the resistance when resistors are connected in series?
questions.explanation: In series, total resistance is the sum: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...

questions.question_text: What is momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum (p) = mass × velocity. It's a vector quantity.

answers.answer_text: p = ½mv² (half mass times velocity squared)

questions.question_text: What is the principle of superposition for waves?
questions.explanation: When waves overlap, the resultant displacement equals the sum of individual displacements.

answers.answer_text: When waves overlap, the total displacement is the sum of individual displacements
Waves always cancel each other out
Waves cannot pass through each other

questions.question_text: What is power defined as?
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work or energy transfer: P = W/t or P = E/t.

questions.question_text: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.explanation: The Watt (W) is the SI unit of power. 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.question_text: What is Newton's Third Law?
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

answers.answer_text: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
Objects at rest stay at rest

questions.question_text: What is the frequency of a wave if its period is 0.5 seconds?
questions.explanation: Frequency = 1/Period. So f = 1/0.5 = 2 Hz.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between scalar and vector quantities?
questions.explanation: Scalars have only magnitude (e.g., mass, speed); vectors have both magnitude and direction (e.g., velocity, force).

answers.answer_text: Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction

questions.question_text: What is specific heat capacity?
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K).

answers.answer_text: Energy required to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C
The maximum temperature a substance can reach
The temperature at which a substance melts

questions.question_text: What is the formula for electric power?
questions.explanation: Electric power P = IV = I²R = V²/R, where I is current, V is voltage, R is resistance.

questions.question_text: What causes an object to undergo circular motion?
questions.explanation: Centripetal force, directed toward the center, causes circular motion.

answers.answer_text: Centripetal force directed toward the center

questions.question_text: What is the law of conservation of momentum?
questions.explanation: In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum before = total momentum after.

answers.answer_text: Total momentum in a closed system remains constant
Momentum is only conserved in elastic collisions

questions.question_text: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz), which equals cycles per second (s⁻¹).
